newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium to review para training after allegations.
newsitem.headline: Belgium to review para training after allegations.

text.p: The Belgian military promised on Thursday to review the training of its paratroops after fresh allegations that soldiers behaved badly while serving with U.N. forces in Somalia in 1993 sparked public outrage.

"We will have a critical evaluation of their training. We will also ask for psychological advice. We'll see whether we're not going too far in training them to become 'Rambos' whose values perhaps have shifted in an unacceptable way," chief of staff Admiral Willy Herteleer told Belgian BRTN radio.

Het Laatste Nieuws newspaper had published on Wednesday a picture showing a soldier urinating on the dead body of a Somali. Another photograph had a soldier with his army boot pressed on the head of a dead Somali.
"The paras of shame," La Derniere Heure newspaper said in a front-page banner headline on Thursday.

Herteleer, who warned against generalisations and hoped just a few individuals were concerned, said the decision to review the paratroops' training, taken after the last series of pictures, had been requested by Belgian Defence Minister Jean-Pol Poncelet.
In daily newspaper De Morgen, the minister openly questioned whether the battalion of paratroopers to which the soldiers portrayed in the pictures belonged should be scrapped,

Belgian media said the houses of several soldiers had been searched, including that of a sergeant-major who could be identified on the latest pictures and was now in Brazzaville with a force stationed in Congo to help evacuate nationals from Zaire if the civil war there were to escalate.

A Belgian military court said last week it had arrested one soldier and was investigating others over allegations they tortured children in Somalia following a first series of pictures and stories printed in Het Laatste Nieuws.
"The dossier (with) all the information will be handed to the auditor-general of the court martial and we hope he will find the culprits and have them convicted," Herteleer said.
"Even if a tenth of what has been said is true, it is not acceptable," he added.
Poncelet expressed disgust over the latest pictures. "I'm aghast. This is horrible and tasteless," he was quoted on Wednesday as saying.

An army spokesman has said the urinating soldier was bound to be thrown out of the army if he could be identified but added that the other pictures -- one showing a Belgian soldier in a Somali's grave -- were merely of soldiers in a situation of war.

Colonel Freddy Van de Weghe, commander of Belgium's paratroop brigade, pointed out that during the 12 months of the U.N. "Restore Hope" mission in Somalia the Belgian detachments were confronted several times with combat situations and that six of their men, including five paratroopers, were killed.
A further 15 had been hurt by bullets and grenades.
Belgian troops who served in Somalia have already been repeatedly accused of human rights abuses.
In August 1993, while they were still in the country, there were allegations they had massively understated the number of Somalis they had killed during military operations.

The allegations, by five of the paratroopers, also said the 1,000 Belgian troops based in Kismayu in southern Somalia often fired at armed Somali fighters even if they themselves had not come under attack.
In October 1995 nine Belgian soldiers accused of maltreating Somali children were acquitted by a Brussels miltary court, and another was given an eight-day suspended jail sentence.
